claim: The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae exhibits a Rabl-like orientation during interphase, where centromeres cluster at one end of the nucleus attached to the spindle pole body, and chromosome arms extend outward toward the nuclear periphery where telomeres associate.
source: The predominant feature of yeast 3D genome organization is its Rabl-like orientation (Jin et al., 1998) (Figure 1A): during interphase, the centromeres cluster at one end of the nucleus, attached to the spindle pole body, and chromosome arms extend outward toward the nuclear periphery where the telomeres associate (Schober et al., 2008; Therizols et al., 2010), like in anaphase.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Jin et al., 1998; Schober et al., 2008; Therizols et al., 2010) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The ribosomal DNA array forms the nucleolus opposite the spindle pole, splitting chromosome XII into two separate domains that behave as if they were separate chromosomes.
source: In addition, the ribosomal DNA array forms the nucleolus, opposite the spindle pole (Yang et al., 1989), splitting chromosome XII into two separate domains that behave as if they were separate chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 1989.

claim: The Rabl-like organization largely persists through the cell cycle and even in stationary phase, albeit with increased telomere clustering and decreased centromere clustering.
source: This organization largely persists through the cell cycle (Jin et al., 1998) and even in stationary phase, albeit with increased telomere clustering and decreased centromere clustering (Guidi et al., 2015; Rutledge et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jin et al., 1998; Guidi et al., 2015; Rutledge et al., 2015.

claim: A simple volume-exclusion polymer model of chromosomes in a Rabl-like orientation is sufficient to explain microscopy and Hi-C data of the budding yeast genome in haploids grown under standard lab conditions.
source: However, multiple studies have argued that a simple volume-exclusion polymer model of chromosomes in a Rabl-like orientation is sufficient to explain microscopy and Hi-C data of the budding yeast genome (Tjong et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2012), at least in haploids grown under standard lab conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tjong et al., 2012 and Wong et al., 2012.

claim: Homologous chromosomes can pair in diploid yeast not only in meiosis, but also during mitotic growth.
source: In diploid yeast, homologous chromosomes can pair not only in meiosis, but also during mitotic growth (Burgess and Kleckner, 1999; Burgess et al., 1999; Dekker et al., 2002; Weiner and Kleckner, 1994), as they do in Drosophila (Metz, 1916).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burgess and Kleckner, 1999; Burgess et al., 1999; Dekker et al., 2002; Weiner and Kleckner, 1994; Metz, 1916.

claim: The extent of mitotic homolog pairing has been debated due to discrepancies between studies.
source: However, the extent of mitotic homolog pairing has been debated due to discrepancies between studies (Barzel and Kupiec, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Barzel and Kupiec, 2008.

claim: In fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), signal loss can lead to false inference of colocalization.
source: In fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), signal loss can lead to false inference of colocalization (Lorenz et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lorenz et al., 2003.

claim: Tagging of genomic loci with repetitive arrays of GFP for live-cell imaging can directly cause pairing via GFP dimerization.
source: It has also been suggested that tagging of genomic loci with repetitive arrays of GFP for live-cell imaging can directly cause pairing via GFP dimerization (Mirkin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mirkin et al., 2014.

claim: Genes that respond to signals like galactose induction (GAL1, HXK1), inositol starvation (INO1), oxidative stress, and heat shock (HSP104) relocate to the nuclear periphery upon activation via interactions with nuclear pore complexes.
source: Genes that respond to signals like galactose induction (GAL1, HXK1), inositol starvation (INO1), oxidative stress, and heat shock (HSP104) have been observed by microscopy to relocate to the nuclear periphery upon activation via interactions with nuclear pore complexes (Ahmed et al., 2010; Brickner and Walter, 2004; Brickner et al., 2016; Casolari et al., 2004; Dieppois et al., 2006; Dultz et al., 2016; Taddei et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2010; Brickner and Walter, 2004; Brickner et al., 2016; Casolari et al., 2004; Dieppois et al., 2006; Dultz et al., 2016; Taddei et al., 2006.

claim: Nuclear pore interactions can mediate clustering of genes that share Gene Recruitment Sequences, including homologous alleles.
source: Nuclear pore interactions can mediate clustering of genes that share Gene Recruitment Sequences, including homologous alleles (Brickner et al., 2015, 2012, 2016; Randise-Hinchliff et al., 2016), and even impact the conformation of chromosomes well beyond the induced gene (Dultz et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brickner et al., 2015, 2012, 2016; Randise-Hinchliff et al., 2016; Dultz et al., 2016.

claim: Divergent Saccharomyces species can form stable hybrids, such as between S. cerevisiae and S. paradoxus (90% nucleotide identity in coding regions) or S. uvarum (80% nucleotide identity in coding regions).
source: However, divergent Saccharomyces species can form stable hybrids (González et al., 2006; Mertens et al., 2015), e.g. between S. cerevisiae and S. paradoxus (90% nucleotide identity in coding regions [Kellis et al., 2003]) or its more distant relative S. uvarum (also known as S. bayanus var. uvarum; 80% nucleotide identity in coding regions [Kellis et al., 2003]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to González et al., 2006; Mertens et al., 2015; Kellis et al., 2003.

claim: Interspecific hybrids between diverged Saccharomyces species are sufficiently diverged to allow straightforward sequence-level discrimination of homologs.
source: These interspecific hybrids are sufficiently diverged to allow straightforward sequence-level discrimination of homologs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) but have maintained nearly complete synteny (Fischer et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Fischer et al., 2000.

claim: Hi-C data from diploid yeast exhibit signatures of a Rabl-like orientation, including frequent intrachromosomal interactions between adjacent loci, pericentromeric regions interacting frequently with one another, and telomeric regions preferentially interacting.
source: The most prominent features of Hi-C data from diploid yeast are the signatures of a Rabl-like orientation (Figure 1C,D). As in all Hi-C datasets, the contact map exhibits a strong diagonal signal indicating frequent intrachromosomal interactions between adjacent loci. In addition, pericentromeric regions interact frequently with one another, but infrequently with regions far from centromeres, as expected from the clustering of centromeres at the spindle pole body. Telomeric regions also preferentially interact, consistent with their clustering at the nuclear periphery.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C,D and description of observed Hi-C patterns.

claim: The rDNA-carrying chromosomes each behave as two separate chromosomes divided by the nucleolus, with frequent interactions on either side of the rDNA array but not across it.
source: Finally, the rDNA-carrying chromosomes each behave as two separate chromosomes divided by the nucleolus, with frequent interactions on either side of the rDNA array but not across it.
evidence: The claim is based on Hi-C data observations described in the manuscript.

claim: An off-diagonal line of increased interaction in Hi-C data is suggestive of homolog pairing.
source: In addition to these previously described phenomena, we observed an off-diagonal line of increased interaction suggestive of homolog pairing (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on Hi-C data observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Homologous loci tend to be closer together than nonhomologous loci in multiple assays, including microscopy, recombination efficiency, and chromatin conformation capture.
source: Homologous loci tend to be closer together than nonhomologous loci in multiple assays, including microscopy (Burgess et al., 1999; Weiner and Kleckner, 1994), recombination efficiency (Burgess and Kleckner, 1999), and chromatin conformation capture (Dekker et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 1999; Weiner and Kleckner, 1994; Burgess and Kleckner, 1999; Dekker et al., 2002.

claim: After controlling for the Rabl-like orientation by restricting comparisons to interactions with loci at similar distance from the centromere and on chromosome arms of similar length, the observed interaction between homologous alleles exceeds that predicted based on the Rabl-like orientation.
source: Even with these stringent constraints, we find that the observed interaction between homologous alleles exceeds that predicted based on the Rabl-like orientation (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E comparing experimental data to polymer model predictions.

claim: The left arm of chromosome III and the right arm of chromosome IX exhibit particularly strong homolog proximity.
source: Of note, the left arm of chromosome III and the right arm of chromosome IX exhibit particularly strong homolog proximity (Figure 2B); proximity at chromosome III is possibly due to pairing of the silenced mating-type loci (Miele et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Miele et al., 2009 for the mating-type loci explanation.

claim: Homolog proximity is substantially greater in saturated cultures approaching stationary phase than in exponential growth in all hybrids tested.
source: In all hybrids, homolog proximity is substantially greater in saturated cultures approaching stationary phase than in exponential growth (Figure 2E), consistent with previous observations (Burgess et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and citation to Burgess et al., 1999.

claim: Nocodazole arrest does not substantially reduce homolog proximity in the diverged hybrid S. cerevisiae x S. uvarum.
source: We find that nocodazole arrest does not substantially reduce homolog proximity in the diverged hybrid S. cerevisiae x S. uvarum (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In polymer models of the Rabl-like orientation, smaller nuclear size led to decreased, rather than increased, homolog proximity.
source: In these models, smaller nuclear size led to decreased, rather than increased, homolog proximity (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by polymer model simulations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The difference in homolog proximity between saturated and exponentially growing cultures cannot be explained by the effect of differences in nuclear size.
source: These models suggest that the difference in homolog proximity between saturated and exponentially growing cultures cannot be explained by the effect of differences in nuclear size, and provide additional support for homolog pairing beyond the Rabl-like orientation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from polymer model simulations.

claim: GAL1 and its neighbors GAL7 and GAL10 move upon galactose induction from their location near the spindle pole body to a nuclear pore complex at the nuclear periphery.
source: This gene and its neighbors GAL7 and GAL10 move upon galactose induction from their location near the spindle pole body to a nuclear pore complex at the nuclear periphery (Casolari et al., 2004; Dultz et al., 2016) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Casolari et al., 2004; Dultz et al., 2016 and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Both GAL1 loci interacted less with pericentromeric regions upon galactose induction.
source: Consistent with this expectation, we found using Hi-C that both GAL1 loci interacted less with pericentromeric regions upon galactose induction (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 3B–D.

claim: Markedly increased interactions between homologous loci surrounding the genes HAS1 and TDA1 on chromosome XIII occur under both growth saturation and galactose induction, compared to standard exponential growth in glucose.
source: Surprisingly, we observed markedly increased interactions between homologous loci surrounding the genes HAS1 and TDA1 (subsequently abbreviated as 'HAS1-TDA1 loci') on chromosome XIII under both growth saturation and galactose induction, compared to standard exponential growth in glucose (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Under inducing conditions, the interaction between HAS1-TDA1 homologs is among the strongest genome-wide, excluding pericentromeric and subtelomeric regions.
source: In fact, under inducing conditions, this interaction is among the strongest genome-wide, excluding pericentromeric and subtelomeric regions (top interaction out of over 83,000; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inducible homolog proximity at HAS1-TDA1 appears to be evolutionarily conserved, as it occurs in all three tested interspecific hybrids, at least in saturated culture.
source: Nevertheless, this inducible homolog proximity appears to be evolutionarily conserved, as it occurs in all three tested interspecific hybrids, at least in saturated culture (Figure 4A–C; galactose not tested in all hybrids).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Every deletion that included the HAS1pr-TDA1pr intergenic region reduced the interaction frequency between HAS1-TDA1 homologs in saturated growth conditions back to uninduced levels.
source: Every deletion that included this intergenic region reduced the interaction frequency between HAS1-TDA1 homologs in saturated growth conditions back to uninduced levels, indicating that this inducible pairing is sequence-dependent (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data from deletion strains shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of the HAS1 coding sequence had minimal impact on HAS1-TDA1 pairing, showing that the deletion construct itself did not impede inducible pairing.
source: In contrast, deletion of the HAS1 coding sequence had minimal impact, which shows that the deletion construct itself did not impede inducible pairing (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data from deletion strains shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ectopic HAS1pr-TDA1pr allele exhibited inducible interactions with the S. uvarum HAS1pr-TDA1pr, although not to the same extent as the endogenous allele.
source: The ectopic HAS1pr-TDA1pr allele exhibited inducible interactions with the S. uvarum HAS1pr-TDA1pr, although not to the same extent as the endogenous allele (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: In homozygous S. cerevisiae diploids, the HAS1-TDA1 homologs were closer together in galactose-induced and saturated cultures than in glucose, as measured by confocal microscopy.
source: Consistent with our Hi-C data, the HAS1-TDA1 homologs were closer together in galactose-induced and saturated cultures than in glucose (Figure 4G,H and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4G,H and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: The HAS1-TDA1 locus shifted to the nuclear periphery upon galactose induction and in saturated culture conditions in haploid S. cerevisiae.
source: Indeed, the HAS1-TDA1 locus shifted to the nuclear periphery upon galactose induction and in saturated culture conditions (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: Nup2 but not Nup100 was required for peripheral localization of the HAS1-TDA1 locus.
source: As in other cases of gene relocalization, Nup2 but not Nup100 was required for peripheral localization of the HAS1-TDA1 locus.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data from deletion strains shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Unlike other relocalized genes, HAS1-TDA1 locus relocalization did not require Mlp2.
source: However, unlike other relocalized genes (Ahmed et al., 2010; Brickner et al., 2016; Luthra et al., 2007), HAS1-TDA1 locus relocalization did not require Mlp2, suggesting that the HAS1-TDA1 locus may interact with nuclear pores via a distinct mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data from deletion strains shown in Figure 5A and citations to Ahmed et al., 2010; Brickner et al., 2016; Luthra et al., 2007.

claim: The HAS1-TDA1 loci are peripherally relocalized in diploids.
source: Thus, we confirmed that the HAS1-TDA1 loci are peripherally relocalized in diploids, by reanalyzing the images we used to measure distances between HAS1-TDA1 alleles in diploid cells (Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 2.

claim: HAS1-TDA1 alleles can remain paired in galactose in the nucleoplasm.
source: In fact, HAS1-TDA1 alleles can remain paired in galactose in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The peripheral localization of HAS1-TDA1 loci exhibits cell cycle dependence.
source: In agreement with these studies, the peripheral localization of HAS1-TDA1 loci that we observe also exhibits cell cycle dependence (Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—source data 2), which may explain the presence of pairing in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—source data 2.

claim: Nup2 is required for HAS1-TDA1 homolog pairing in galactose but not in saturated growth.
source: In this strain, HAS1-TDA1 pairing was not observed in galactose, as expected, but still occurred at full strength in saturated growth (Figure 5F). These data indicate that Nup2 is required for HAS1-TDA1 homolog pairing in galactose but not in saturated culture, suggesting distinct and/or additional mechanisms of pairing.
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data from nup2Δ strains shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Nup60 ChIP-seq showed clear enrichment of the galactose metabolism gene cluster GAL1-GAL10-GAL7 in the immunoprecipitated DNA from cells grown in galactose, compared to those grown in glucose.
source: As expected, we observed a clear enrichment of the galactose metabolism gene cluster GAL1-GAL10-GAL7 in the immunoprecipitated DNA from cells grown in galactose, compared to those grown in glucose (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Nup60 ChIP-seq showed little if any enrichment of the HAS1-TDA1 locus.
source: In contrast, we observed little if any such enrichment of the HAS1-TDA1 locus (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: HAS1 is downregulated in both galactose and saturated growth conditions.
source: HAS1 is downregulated in both pairing conditions (Figure 6A), whereas TDA1 is weakly upregulated in both conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TDA1 is weakly upregulated in both galactose and saturated growth conditions.
source: HAS1 is downregulated in both pairing conditions (Figure 6A), whereas TDA1 is weakly upregulated in both conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Transcriptional changes at HAS1 and TDA1 are relatively unremarkable; in both galactose and saturated growth, dozens to hundreds of genes are more strongly up- or downregulated than HAS1 or TDA1.
source: However, transcriptional changes at HAS1 and TDA1 are relatively unremarkable; in both galactose and saturated growth, dozens to hundreds of genes are more strongly up- or downregulated than HAS1 or TDA1 (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: GAL1 is upregulated nearly 1000-fold in galactose.
source: For example, GAL1 is upregulated nearly 1000-fold in galactose (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: After using a polymer model of the Rabl-like orientation to calibrate estimates, homologous chromosomes do interact preferentially during mitotic growth in hybrid diploids with homologs diverged to less than 80% nucleotide identity, albeit subtly.
source: After using a polymer model of the Rabl-like orientation to calibrate our estimates, we find that even in hybrid diploids with homologs diverged to less than 80% nucleotide identity, homologous chromosomes do interact preferentially during mitotic growth, albeit subtly (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data compared to polymer model predictions shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Homolog pairing strength depends on both growth conditions and genomic location.
source: Homolog pairing strength also depends on both growth conditions and genomic location, sometimes jointly: the homologous HAS1-TDA1 loci on chromosome XIII pairs during saturated growth and galactose induction, but not exponential growth in glucose (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The HAS1-TDA1 region is not remarkably conserved, suggesting that homolog pairing is at least partly due to specific interactions mediated by proteins, rather than direct DNA-DNA homology interactions.
source: This region is not remarkably conserved, suggesting that homolog pairing is at least partly due to specific interactions mediated by proteins, rather than direct DNA-DNA homology interactions (Danilowicz et al., 2009; Gladyshev and Kleckner, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of conservation and citations to Danilowicz et al., 2009; Gladyshev and Kleckner, 2014.

claim: Nuclear pore interactions may confine the HAS1-TDA1 alleles to the relatively small space near the nuclear periphery, thus speeding up the rate at which they randomly contact each other.
source: Regardless of the molecular mechanism, nuclear pore interactions may confine the HAS1-TDA1 alleles to the relatively small space near the nuclear periphery, thus speeding up the rate at which they randomly contact each other (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism, supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Additional mechanisms such as protein-protein interactions between DNA-binding proteins could prolong the duration of contact between HAS1-TDA1 alleles, even after the alleles are no longer at a nuclear pore.
source: Once in physical proximity, additional mechanisms such as protein-protein interactions between DNA-binding proteins could prolong the duration of contact, even after the alleles are no longer at a nuclear pore.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: The presence of paired HAS1-TDA1 alleles in the nucleoplasm suggests that nuclear pore-independent pairing mechanisms may act at HAS1-TDA1.
source: Indeed, the presence of paired HAS1-TDA1 alleles in the nucleoplasm suggests that such nuclear pore-independent pairing mechanisms may act at HAS1-TDA1 (Figure 5C and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—source data 2.

claim: A recent study showed that Nup2 is involved in meiotic homolog pairing, suggesting that Nup2 may more generally play a role in homolog pairing.
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed that Nup2 is involved in meiotic homolog pairing (Chu et al., 2017), suggesting that Nup2 may more generally play a role in homolog pairing.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chu et al., 2017 and inference about general role.

claim: Divergence between S. cerevisiae and S. uvarum, particularly in their galactose metabolism pathways, may contribute to the lack of pairing at the GAL1 locus.
source: Divergence between S. cerevisiae and S. uvarum, particularly in their galactose metabolism pathways (Roop et al., 2016), may also contribute to the lack of pairing at the GAL1 locus.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Roop et al., 2016.

claim: Tda1 is a kinase required for phosphorylation of Hxk2, the primary hexokinase in yeast.
source: Tda1 is a kinase required for phosphorylation of Hxk2, the primary hexokinase in yeast (Kaps et al., 2015; Kettner et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kaps et al., 2015; Kettner et al., 2012.

claim: Unphosphorylated Hxk2 can interact with Mig1 to repress various alternative carbon source metabolism genes in the presence of glucose.
source: Unphosphorylated Hxk2 can interact with Mig1 to repress various alternative carbon source metabolism genes in the presence of glucose.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Hxk2 and Mig1 function.

claim: Phosphorylation of Hxk2 by Tda1 in low-glucose conditions prevents its interaction with Mig1 and thus leads to release from glucose repression.
source: Phosphorylation of Hxk2 by Tda1 in low-glucose conditions prevents its interaction with Mig1 and thus leads to release from glucose repression.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Tda1, Hxk2, and Mig1 function.

claim: Nuclear pore interaction may aid the upregulation of TDA1 in response to low-glucose concentrations, perhaps by facilitating efficient transcription or mRNA export from the nucleus.
source: While we have not yet tested whether disrupting peripheral localization would affect TDA1 or HAS1 transcription, we hypothesize that nuclear pore interaction may aid the upregulation of TDA1 in response to low-glucose concentrations, perhaps by facilitating efficient transcription or mRNA export from the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about potential function.

claim: Increased transcription may itself contribute to localization at nuclear pores via interactions between nascent mRNA and mRNA processing and export factors at nuclear pores.
source: Increased transcription may itself contribute to localization at nuclear pores via interactions between nascent mRNA and mRNA processing and export factors at nuclear pores (Akhtar and Gasser, 2007), and may be involved in establishment of HAS1-TDA1 pairing as it is for GAL1 (Brickner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citations to Akhtar and Gasser, 2007; Brickner et al., 2016.

claim: For some genes, nuclear pore interactions mediate rapid reactivation in a phenomenon termed epigenetic transcriptional memory.
source: For some genes, nuclear pore interactions mediate rapid reactivation in a phenomenon termed epigenetic transcriptional memory (D'Urso and Brickner, 2017; D'Urso et al., 2016; Light et al., 2010); it is also possible that the nuclear pore interactions with HAS1-TDA1 may be involved in epigenetic transcriptional memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to D'Urso and Brickner, 2017; D'Urso et al., 2016; Light et al., 2010.

claim: The pairing of the HAS1-TDA1 alleles may serve a distinct function, potentially including trans gene regulation like at GAL1.
source: The pairing of the HAS1-TDA1 alleles may also serve a distinct function, potentially including trans gene regulation like at GAL1 (Zhang and Bai, 2016), but further experiments are needed to test this possibility.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Zhang and Bai, 2016.

claim: Recent studies in the fruit fly Drosophila have provided evidence for the generality of the role of nuclear pores in transcriptional regulation first observed in yeast.
source: While yeast nuclear organization may differ from that of other eukaryotes in some ways, our findings may, nevertheless, be applicable to other organisms: recent studies in the fruit fly Drosophila have provided evidence for the generality of the role of nuclear pores in transcriptional regulation first observed in yeast (Pascual-Garcia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pascual-Garcia et al., 2017.

claim: The diploid yeast genome has a dynamic and complex 3D organization.
source: Together, these results reveal that the diploid yeast genome has a dynamic and complex 3D organization.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the study.

claim: Homolog proximity increases in saturated culture conditions after controlling for the Rabl-like orientation using a polymer model.
source: After controlling for the Rabl-like orientation using a polymer model, we observe significant homolog proximity that increases in saturated culture conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing experimental results to polymer model predictions.

claim: A localized increase in homologous interactions between the HAS1-TDA1 alleles occurs specifically under galactose induction and saturated growth.
source: Surprisingly, we observe a localized increase in homologous interactions between the HAS1-TDA1 alleles specifically under galactose induction and saturated growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by Hi-C data showing condition-specific pairing.

claim: HAS1-TDA1 pairing is accompanied by relocalization to the nuclear periphery and requires Nup2, suggesting a role for nuclear pore complexes.
source: This pairing is accompanied by relocalization to the nuclear periphery and requires Nup2, suggesting a role for nuclear pore complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and Hi-C data from deletion strains.
